FINDING_ID: R3_F001  
SEVERITY: 0.89  
FLAW_CLASS: 5 (correctness)  
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.83  
VERIFIED: TRUE  
DESCRIPTION: `DynamicManager.process_round()` records failures only for models present in `responses`, but then computes convergence/diminishing-returns from the global `findings` list as if the round were complete. If an allocated model never responds and is simply absent from `responses`, no failure is detected, no recovery is triggered, `active_models` is unchanged, and the round can still advance normally. This creates a cross-area soundness hole: the failure layer treats missing responses as success-by-omission, while the FSM is advanced with `round_complete=True` unconditionally and the convergence logic consumes a potentially partial evidence set. The system therefore misclassifies incomplete rounds as complete and can terminate or converge on censored data.

FINDING_ID: R3_F002  
SEVERITY: 0.85  
FLAW_CLASS: 1 (logic)  
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.80  
VERIFIED: TRUE  
DESCRIPTION: `DynamicManager.process_round()` accepts arbitrary `responses` and `findings` without checking that they belong to `self.fsm.current_round`. It uses `round_idx = self.fsm.current_round` for bookkeeping, but neither `response.round_idx` nor `finding.round_idx` is validated against it. A caller can accidentally submit stale or future-round artifacts, and the manager will attribute them to the current FSM round in convergence, failure history, eventing, and fingerprint updates. This is a cross-cutting temporal-integrity bug affecting Areas 3, 4, 5, and 6 simultaneously.

FINDING_ID: R3_F003  
SEVERITY: 0.82  
FLAW_CLASS: 2 (interface)  
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.78  
VERIFIED: TRUE  
DESCRIPTION: The orchestration contract around allocation is internally inconsistent. `DynamicManager.get_allocation()` computes an allocation, but `process_round()` discards allocation entirely (`RoundResult.allocation=None`) and performs no validation that `responses` correspond to allocated models/tasks. As a result, load-balancing decisions are not causally linked to failure detection, convergence accounting, or diminishing-returns cost attribution. The manager can process responses from models that were never allocated work, or fail to notice silent non-responses from models that were allocated work. This is more than a missing field: it breaks the data lineage between Area 2 and the rest of the management layer.

FINDING_ID: R3_F004  
SEVERITY: 0.78  
FLAW_CLASS: 5 (correctness)  
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.74  
VERIFIED: TRUE  
DESCRIPTION: `LoadBalancer.solve()` computes pre-dispatch feasibility only through the standalone `dispatch_check()` helper, but the actual allocation algorithm `_solve_greedy()` and feasibility checker `_check_feasibility()` ignore `L_std` and `feasibility_threshold` completely. Thus the advertised probabilistic feasibility extension is not part of solving; the solver may allocate work to a model with low `P(feasible)` and still call the allocation “feasible” as long as deterministic `task_load <= L` holds. This is a cross-area mismatch between the documented hardening feature and the actual dispatch/allocation semantics.

FINDING_ID: R3_F005  
SEVERITY: 0.73  
FLAW_CLASS: 6 (edge-case)  
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.69  
VERIFIED: TRUE  
DESCRIPTION: `LoadBalancer.__init__()` does not validate that every `task_id` and `model_id` is unique, yet `Allocation`, `_model_idx`, and `_task_idx` rely on identity-by-string with overwriting semantics. Duplicate `task_id`s silently collapse in `_task_idx` and `Allocation.model_load()`’s `task_map`; duplicate `model_id`s silently collapse in `_model_idx`, `role_map`, `responses`, `findings` grouping, and failure history. The result is silent aliasing rather than a clean error, and it corrupts allocation, accounting, and recovery behavior across the module.

FINDING_ID: R3_F006  
SEVERITY: 0.70  
FLAW_CLASS: 5 (correctness)  
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.66  
VERIFIED: TRUE  
DESCRIPTION: `RoleAssignment.assign()` and `reassign()` use deterministic tie-breaking only for PM selection and partially for initial COL selection, but `reassign()` chooses `best_col_id = max(col_scores, key=lambda mid: col_scores[mid])` over `remaining_ids` derived from a `set`. When COL scores tie, the winner depends on set iteration order rather than the documented deterministic tie-break rule. This makes dynamic role reassignment nondeterministic across runs/interpreters even though the module claims deterministic management behavior.

FINDING_ID: R3_F007  
SEVERITY: 0.68  
FLAW_CLASS: 6 (edge-case)  
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.63  
VERIFIED: TRUE  
DESCRIPTION: `ConvergenceDetector.add_round_findings()` permits the same `round_idx` to be overwritten silently with a new finding set and duration, invalidating caches for subsequent rounds but not preserving any audit trail or monotonicity constraint. In a distributed or retried orchestration setting, duplicate submissions for the same round can replace prior evidence without warning, changing convergence outcomes retrospectively. Given the module’s role as a management/control layer, silent historical mutation is a substantive edge-case flaw rather than a benign convenience.

FINDING_ID: R3_F008  
SEVERITY: 0.65  
FLAW_CLASS: 1 (logic)  
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.71  
VERIFIED: TRUE  
DESCRIPTION: `FailureHandler.detect_failure()` only emits manager events for EMPTY, TIMEOUT, MALFORMED, and mislabelled FORMAT failures. It emits no event at all for `UNDERPERFORM`, even when that condition is the returned failure type and later drives recovery/escalation. This leaves the “real-time manager monitoring interface” blind to one of the core typed failures that can trigger role downgrade and eventually abort-related decisions. The bug is cross-cutting because the failure subsystem internally observes the condition while the monitoring interface does not.

FINDING_ID: R3_F009  
SEVERITY: 0.61  
FLAW_CLASS: 4 (completeness)  
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.75  
VERIFIED: TRUE  
DESCRIPTION: `DynamicManager.process_round()` emits `ROUND_COMPLETE`, `CONVERGENCE_CHECK`, and `STOP_CHECK` events, but never emits `ROUND_START`, `MODEL_RESPONSE`, `RETRY`, `REALLOCATE`, `EXCLUDE`, or `ABORT` events despite defining them in `ManagerEventType` and documenting dynamic PM monitoring. The event model therefore exposes a richer protocol than the orchestrator actually produces. This is a broader integration miss than the previously noted callback plumbing issues: most of the declared monitoring vocabulary is dead API surface.

FINDING_ID: R3_F010  
SEVERITY: 0.57  
FLAW_CLASS: 6 (edge-case)  
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.58  
VERIFIED: TRUE  
DESCRIPTION: `CapabilityFingerprint.as_normalised_array()` assumes `pool_max` is non-negative and meaningful as a divisor vector, but neither the method nor `ModelSpec` validates fingerprint components. Negative `D_decay`, `v_bar`, `A`, or `C` values propagate into normalization and scoring, and a negative `pool_max[0]` can make the inverted decay term exceed 1 or behave counterintuitively. This is distinct from the already-noted documentation mismatch: the implementation permits invalid capability states that distort role scoring and expected-performance baselines throughout the system.

Definitive stance: there are still materially new findings beyond the prior rounds, primarily around cross-area integrity: missing-response handling, temporal validation, broken allocation lineage, nondeterministic reassignment, and unintegrated probabilistic feasibility.
